prepare-for-lumbar-puncture.title: Prepare For Lumbar Puncture
prepare-for-lumbar-puncture.excerpt: Lumbar puncture is a sterile procedure in which a spinal needle is inserted, between the third and fourth lumbar vertebrae in the lower spine at the

blocks.text: Lumbar puncture is a sterile procedure in which a spinal needle is inserted, between the third and fourth lumbar vertebrae in the lower spine at the subarachnoid space i.e. the space between the spinal cord and its covering, the meninges to obtain samples of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) for qualitative analysis.
The site of the puncture can be between the 3rd and 4th or 4th and 5th Lumbar vertebrae where there is no danger of damaging the spinal cord.
A **lumbar puncture (LP)** is performed for diagnostic, therapeutic, and medication-administration purposes involving **cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)** and the **central nervous system (CNS)**.

blocks.title: Clinical Indications for Lumbar Puncture
rows: **1. Measure CSF pressure**
Measures **cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure**; increased pressure within the skull (**intracranial pressure**) can be a sign of various conditions and helps assess for potential complications.
**2. Assist in diagnosing suspected CNS infections & disorders**
**Bacterial or viral meningitis:** Inflammation of the **meninges** (the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord)
**Meningoencephalitis:** Inflammation of both the meninges and the brain
**Intracranial or subarachnoid hemorrhage:** Bleeding within the skull or the space between the brain and the meninges
**Malignant disorders:** Cancerous conditions affecting the **central nervous system (CNS)**
**3. Evaluate & diagnose demyelinating or inflammatory CNS processes**
**Multiple Sclerosis (MS):** Autoimmune disease affecting the CNS; CSF analysis detects characteristic **oligoclonal bands**
**Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS):** Autoimmune disorder affecting the peripheral nervous system, leading to muscle weakness and paralysis; LP reveals **elevated protein levels** in the CSF
**Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis (ADEM):** Rare inflammatory disease of the brain and spinal cord
**4. Infuse medications & diagnostic contrast**
**Spinal anesthesia before surgery:** Numbs nerves in the spinal canal to provide pain relief during surgery
**Myelography (inject dye):** Contrast material for diagnostic imaging to visualize the spinal canal and nerves
**Cisternography (radioactive substances):** Diagnostic imaging to evaluate the flow of CSF
**Chemotherapy drugs:** Administered directly into the spinal canal to treat certain types of cancer affecting the CNS
**5. Treat normal pressure hydrocephalus**
A condition where excess **CSF** accumulates in the brain, leading to symptoms like **walking difficulties** and **cognitive decline**.
**6. Treat cerebrospinal fistulas**
Abnormal connections between the **CSF space** and other parts of the body.
**7. Treat idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH)**
A condition of **increased pressure within the skull** with no clear cause.
**8. Placement of a lumbar CSF drainage catheter**
A thin tube inserted into the **spinal canal** to drain **excess CSF**.

blocks.text: Contraindications

Warning: **Increased intracranial pressure from a brain tumor or space-occupying lesion** risks **cerebral or cerebellar herniation** with severe neurological deterioration after CSF withdrawal. Obtain a **CT scan or MRI** beforehand when suspected, and never proceed with **severe coagulopathy** (**epidural hematoma** risk) or **skin infection near the puncture site**.

blocks.title: Contraindications to Lumbar Puncture
rows: **Space-occupying lesion**
Obtain a **computerized tomography (CT) scan** or **MRI** prior to lumbar puncture to determine if there is evidence of a space-occupying lesion causing **increased intracranial pressure**.
**Severe coagulopathy or bleeding disorders**
Due to the significant risk of **epidural hematoma** formation.
**Severe degenerative vertebral joint disease**
Difficulty passing the needle through the degenerative arthritic inter-spinal space, such as in **spinal stenosis**.
**Severe spinal deformities**
Patients with severe spinal deformities, such as **scoliosis**, may have an increased risk of complications.
**Skin infection near the puncture site**
Increases the risk of contamination of infected material into the **CSF**.
**Increased intracranial pressure due to a brain tumor**
**Cerebral or cerebellar herniation** with severe neurological deterioration may occur after the withdrawal of **CSF**.
**Patient refusal**
The decision to undergo a lumbar puncture is the **patient’s choice**; if a patient refuses the procedure, their wishes must be respected.

blocks.title: Lumbar Puncture Nursing Procedure Flow
blocks.caption: Sequential workflow from patient preparation and positioning through CSF collection and post-procedure monitoring.

steps.label: Prepare & Position
steps.detail: Offer bedpan, assemble top shelf, expose lumbar area only, and flex spine (sitting on stool or lateral on fracture board).

steps.label: Asepsis & Anesthesia
steps.detail: Wash hands, don gloves, pour antiseptic, and assist the doctor to cleanse, drape, and administer local anesthesia.

steps.label: Puncture & Collect CSF
steps.detail: Maintain flexion during L3–L4 or L4–L5 puncture; hold specimen bottles 1 cm below needle and provide manometer if needed.

steps.label: Seal & Label
steps.detail: Seal site with tincture benzoin or collodion, apply dressing, label specimens, and send with lab request form.

steps.label: Post-Care & Monitor
steps.detail: Keep patient flat (12–24 hrs), monitor 1/4, 1/2, 1, 2, and 4 hourly for 24 hrs, clear trolley, wash hands, and document.

blocks.title: Step-by-Step Procedure and Rationale
rows: Follow the **general rules**.
Offer a **bedpan** to the patient.
To promote **comfort**.
Position the patient in either of the following positions:
**i. Sitting position:** Sit up on a stool and bend forward with the head between the knees.

**ii. Lateral position:** Lie in a lateral position with the buttocks close to the edge of the bed, knees and hips fully flexed and drawn towards the chin, with one pillow placed under the head; provide a **fracture board**.
A **flexed position** increases the space between the vertebrae. A **hard surface** prevents sagging in the bed and interference with the procedure.
Encourage the patient to **remain in a flexed position** until the procedure is completed.
Prevent **risk of trauma**.
Leave the patient covered and expose **only the lumbar region**.
To provide **privacy**.
Provide **good light** at the lumbar region.
To see the **right site** clearly.
Assemble the requirements for the **top shelf of the trolley**.
Promote **easy access**.
Pour **antiseptic lotion** into one of the gallipots, and the doctor cleanses the puncture site then drapes the area.
For **infection prevention and control**.
**Wash hands**, dry, and put on **gloves**.
To maintain **sterility**.
Assist the doctor in cleaning the lumbar region, giving **local anaesthesia**, and performing the lumbar puncture between the **3rd and 4th (L3–L4)** or **4th and 5th (L4–L5) lumbar vertebrae**.
Promote **success of the procedure** and prevent **injury to the spinal cord**.
Unscrew the **specimen bottles** and place them about **1 cm below the needle** to receive the **cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)**.
To **avoid contamination**.
Reassure the patient and observe the **condition, colour, pulse, and respiration rate**, and report any changes or complaints.
To **detect complications on time**.
**Label the specimens** and take them to the laboratory with a **laboratory request form**.
For **diagnosis of causative organisms**.
Assist the doctor to seal the puncture site with **tincture benzoin or collodion** and apply the **dressing**.
To **prevent leakage of CSF**.
Instruct the patient to stay confined to bed in a **flat position** and to be moved only if necessary for **at least 12 hours**.
To avoid complications like **severe headache and backache**.
Clear away the **used equipment**.
To promote **ward maintenance**.
Monitor the patient’s condition **1/4, 1/2, 1, 2, and 4 hourly for 24 hours** depending on the patient’s condition.
To **detect complications** and manage appropriately.
Clear away the **trolley** and **wash hands**.
To prevent the **spread of infections**.
**Document** the procedure.
To promote **follow-up**.

blocks.text: Points to Remember
**CSF Pressure Measurement:** A **manometer** is given to the doctor to measure **CSF** when required.
**Aseptic Technique:** Extreme care is taken to ensure **aseptic technique** throughout the procedure.
**Flat Bed Rest:** Encourage the patient to remain in a **flat position in bed for 24 hours** (at least **12 hours** minimum).

Clinical Pearl: **Maintain spinal flexion between L3–L4 or L4–L5** until needle removal to prevent trauma, hold open specimen bottles **1 cm below the needle** to avoid contamination, and keep the patient **flat in bed for 12–24 hours** to reduce the risk of **severe headache and backache**.
Before the Procedure
**Explain the procedure to the patient:** Inform the patient about the purpose of the lumbar puncture, the procedure details, where it will be done, and who will perform it.
**Obtain informed consent:** Ensure the patient signs a consent form if required by the institution.
**Reinforce diet:** Advise the patient that fasting is not required.
**Promote comfort:** Instruct the patient to empty the bladder and bowel before the procedure.
**Establish baseline assessment data:** Perform vital signs monitoring and a neurologic assessment of the legs, including movement, strength, and sensation.

**Position the client:** Assist the client to assume a lateral decubitus (fetal) position near the side of the bed with the neck, hips, and knees drawn up to the chest. Alternatively, have the patient sit on the edge of the bed while leaning over a bedside table.
**Instruct to remain still:** Emphasize that the patient must lie very still throughout the procedure to prevent traumatic injury.
During the Procedure
Arrange the equipment for use as per the doctor’s convenience.
**Protect the bed:** Use a mackintosh and draw sheet.
Position the patient for easy access.
Provide a stool for the doctor to sit on during the procedure.
Expose the site to be punctured.
Help monitor the patient’s condition.
Maintain the patient’s position.
Reassure the patient to stay calm during the procedure.
After the Procedure
**Apply brief pressure to the puncture site:** To avoid bleeding, apply pressure and cover the site with a small occlusive dressing or band-aid.
**Place the patient flat on the bed:** The patient should remain flat for 4 to 6 hours, as instructed by the physician, and may turn from side to side without elevating the head.
Monitor vital signs, neurologic status, and intake and output: Assess these every 4 hours for 24 hours to evaluate the patient’s condition.

**Monitor the puncture site:** Watch for signs of CSF leakage and drainage of blood, including positional headaches, nausea, vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia, imbalance, tinnitus, and phonophobia.
**Encourage increased fluid intake:** Advise the patient to drink up to 3,000 ml of fluids in 24 hours to replace the CSF removed during the lumbar puncture.
Label and number the specimen tube correctly: Ensure all samples are properly labeled and sent to the laboratory immediately for evaluation.
**Administer analgesia as ordered:** Provide pain relief for headaches that may occur after the procedure.
**Pressure:** 70 to 180 mm H2O.
**Appearance:** CSF is normally clear and colorless.
**CSF total protein:** 15-45 mg/dL.
**Gamma globulin:** 3 to 12% of the total protein.
**CSF glucose:** 50 to 80 mg/dL.
**CSF cell count:** No red blood cells (RBCs); 0-5 white blood cells (WBCs) per microliter, all mononuclear.
**CSF chloride:** 118 to 130 mEq/L.
The lumbar puncture procedure must be performed with extreme care and aseptic technique to avoid complications such as:
**Headache:** Commonly due to leakage of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) into nearby tissues, affecting around 25% of patients.
**Meningitis:** Infection of the protective membranes covering the brain and spinal cord.
**Bleeding into the Spinal Canal:** Hemorrhage that may cause nerve damage or other complications.
**Sudden Death:** Rare but severe complication, often due to increased intracranial pressure.
**Medullary Compression:** Pressure on the spinal cord, which can lead to neurological issues.
**Edema or Hematoma at the Puncture Site:** Swelling or blood collection at the puncture site.
**CSF Leakage:** Leakage through the dural defect after needle withdrawal.
**Reaction to Anesthesia:** Adverse effects due to the anesthesia used during the procedure.
**Epidural or Subdural Abscess:** Infection in the space around the spinal cord.
**Transient Difficulty in Voiding:** Temporary difficulty in urination post-procedure.
**Transillar Herniation:** Displacement of brain tissue due to pressure changes.
**Local Pain:** Caused by nerve root irritation during the procedure.
**Post-Lumbar Puncture Headache:** Occurs in about 25% of patients due to CSF leakage.
**Back Discomfort or Pain:** Pain at the site of the puncture.
**Brainstem Herniation:** Caused by increased intracranial pressure due to conditions like brain tumors.
Prevention of Post-Lumbar Puncture Headache
To prevent post-lumbar puncture headache, consider the following measures:
**Avoid Strong Light:** Keep the room darkened to reduce discomfort.
**Hydration:** Encourage the patient to drink plenty of fluids to stabilize CSF levels.
**Analgesics:** Provide pain relief medication as prescribed.
Foot of the Bed Raised (Trendelenburg Position ): Elevate the foot of the bed to reduce CSF leakage and pressure on the puncture site.
Use **Lumbar Puncture** as a practical nursing topic, not only a memorized definition. Turn the topic into practical nursing knowledge: meaning, assessment, care priorities, teaching and evaluation.
**What to understand first:** define lumbar puncture, identify the normal or expected pattern, then explain what changes when the patient is unwell.
**Why it matters in care:** the nurse must recognize risk early, explain findings clearly, document accurately and know when to escalate.
**How to revise it:** connect each point to assessment, nursing diagnosis or care problem, intervention, rationale and evaluation.

Findings that are normal, abnormal or urgent.
Resources, referral needs and documentation requirements.
Protect safety, comfort, dignity and infection prevention.
Provide clear care, education and escalation when needed.
Evaluate response and record what changed.
The rationale for these priorities is patient safety: nursing actions should prevent deterioration, reduce discomfort, support recovery and create clear evidence for the next caregiver.
**Expected outcome:** The topic is understood in a way that supports safe nursing judgement and revision.
Explain lumbar puncture in simple language the patient or caregiver can repeat back.
Teach warning signs, medicine or follow-up instructions, hygiene or lifestyle points where relevant.

naso-gastric-tube-and-tube-feeding.title: Naso-Gastric Tube and Tube Feeding
naso-gastric-tube-and-tube-feeding.excerpt: Naso-gastric feeding can be given in two ways:
headings: Feeding the patient using a naso-gastric tube (PEX 2.1.10 - Continued)

blocks.text: A **naso-gastric (NG) tube** is indicated for patients requiring **enteral nutrition**, **gastric decompression**, **lavage**, or **diagnostic sampling** when oral intake is unsafe or impossible:
**Unconscious** patients unable to protect their airway or swallow safely.
After **operations in the mouth, pharynx, or larynx**.
**Obstruction or stricture of the oesophagus** due to **inflammation** or **tumour**.
Severe **dysphagia** (difficulty swallowing).
Babies who are **too weak to feed or to suck**.
Severely **burnt** patients (due to **increased metabolic needs** or inability to take oral feeds).
**Mentally ill** patients who cannot eat.
In cases of persistent **nausea and vomiting** (to **decompress the stomach** or provide **nutrition**).
**Gastric lavage** (washing out the stomach).
Collection of **gastric specimens**.

blocks.title: Equipment and Supplies for NG Tube Insertion
rows: **Trolley (Top Shelf)**
**Sterile naso-gastric tubes:** Appropriate size in a bowl
**Bowl of warm water:** To soften the tube before insertion
**Gallipot with gauze swabs:** For cleaning and handling
**Orange sticks:** Or **nasal speculum** if needed for nostril inspection
**Receiver (kidney dish) with blue litmus paper:** To test gastric aspirate acidity
**Mackintosh cape and towel:** Or dressing mackintosh to protect the patient
**10 ml syringe:** To aspirate gastric contents and inject air
**Spigot or clamp:** To occlude the tube end
**Cup of water:** For rinsing the patient's mouth
**Vomit bowl (kidney dish):** In case of gagging or vomiting
**Strapping (adhesive tape):** To secure the tube
**Receiver:** For used swabs and materials
**Bedside**
**Hand washing equipment:** Access to sink, soap, water, and towel
**Screens:** For privacy
**Stethoscope:** For checking placement
**Patient's chart:** For checking order and documentation
**Waste receptacle:** For safe disposal of waste

blocks.title: Naso-Gastric Tube Insertion Workflow
blocks.caption: Five-stage sequence for safe naso-gastric tube placement.

steps.label: Position & Assess
steps.detail: Position upright or 45° lateral, inspect and clean nostrils, wash hands, and wear clean gloves.

steps.label: Measure & Lubricate
steps.detail: Measure nose-to-earlobe-to-xiphoid length, mark with tape, and lubricate 4–6 inches of tip.

steps.label: Insert & Advance
steps.detail: Direct backward and downward; flex head forward and swallow repeatedly until marked length.

steps.label: Confirm Placement
steps.detail: Verify via aspirate acidity (blue litmus turns red), 10–20 ml air auscultation, or X-ray.

steps.label: Secure & Document
steps.detail: Tape firmly without pressure points, clamp with spigot or drain, clear away, and document.

blocks.title: Step-by-Step Procedure and Rationales (NG Tube Insertion)
rows: **Step 1**
Observe the **general rules**.
Promotes adherence to **standards** and **patient safety**.
**Step 2**
Assist the patient to be in a **sitting-up position**, or a **lateral position** if unconscious but slightly raised to an angle of about **45°**.
Promotes patient ability to **swallow** during the procedure.
**Step 4**
Assess the **patency of the nostrils** and clean the nostrils using **orange sticks** or **gauze**.
Identify the preferred nostril (usually the more patent one).
Facilitates **easy passage** of the tube and promotes **hygiene**.
**Step 5**
**Wash hands** and put on **clean gloves**.
Minimizes the risk of **infection**.
**Step 6**
**Measure the required length** of the tube to insert: from the **tip of the nose** to the **ear lobe**, and then down to the **xiphoid process** (chest bone).
**Mark the measured distance** on the tube with a small piece of **tape**.
Ensures that the tube reaches the **stomach**.
**Step 7**
**Lubricate the tip of the tube** (about **4–6 inches**) with **KY jelly** or **warm water**.
Ensures **easy insertion** and prevents **traumatizing the mucous membranes**.
**Step 8**
Select the clear nostril and **insert the lubricated tube gently**, directing it **backward and downward**.
Follows the **natural passage** and prevents **trauma**.
**Step 9**

Once the tube reaches the **nasopharynx** (usually felt as resistance or gagging), ask the conscious patient to **bend their head slightly forward** (chin to chest) and **swallow repeatedly** (dry swallows or sips of water).
Advance the tube as the patient swallows.
**Swallowing closes the epiglottis** over the trachea and helps guide the tube into the **esophagus**.
Bending the head forward helps close the **airway entrance**.
**Step 10**
If the patient **coughs or shows signs of respiratory distress** (**cyanosis**, **inability to speak**), the tube may be in the **trachea**.
**Withdraw the tube immediately**, allow the patient to recover, and re-attempt insertion.
Prevents **choking** and **aspiration**.
**Step 11**
Continue passing the tube until the **measured length** is reached; if there is any resistance, **rotate the tube gently** and avoid using force.
Forcing against resistance can cause **trauma** to mucosa and cause **anxiety**.
**Step 12**
Secure the tube **temporarily** with tape while checking for placement.
Prevents **displacement** while confirming location.
**Step 13**
**a. Aspirate stomach contents:** Use a syringe and test aspirates with **blue litmus paper** (turns **red** if acidic, indicating gastric placement).
**b. Inject air:** Inject **10–20 ml of air** into the tube while listening over the stomach area with a **stethoscope** for a **whooshing or bubbling sound**.
**c. X-ray confirmation:** Most reliable method, especially for critical patients or those at high risk of aspiration.
Aspiration of contents provides **evidence of placement**.
Testing pH confirms the **acidic environment** of the stomach.
Hearing air confirms the location in the stomach.
**X-ray** is definitive.
**Step 14**
Once placement is confirmed, **secure the tube firmly** to the patient's **nose or cheek** with **adhesive tape**, avoiding pressure points and ensuring the tape is not too tight.
Secures the tube in position and prevents **dislodgement**.
**Step 15**
**Clamp the end of the tube** with a **spigot** or connect it to a **drainage bag** if the purpose is drainage or decompression.
Prevents **leakage** or allows **continuous drainage**.
**Step 16**
**Clear away the equipment**, ensure the patient is comfortable, and **wash hands**.
Maintains **cleanliness** and **patient comfort**.
**Step 17**
**Document the procedure** in full:

**Include:** Date, time, **type and size of tube**, **nostril used**, **measured length**, **method of placement confirmation**, **amount and characteristics of aspirate** (if any), **patient's response**, and **name/signature of nurse**.
Promotes **follow-up** and ensures **continuity of care**.

blocks.text: Warning: **Airway Misplacement Risk:** If the patient coughs, develops **cyanosis**, or cannot speak during insertion, the tube may be in the **trachea**. **Withdraw the tube immediately** and let the patient recover before re-attempting.

Clinical Pearl: **Placement Verification:** **Blue litmus paper turning red** confirms gastric acidity, whereas **X-ray confirmation** is the definitive standard for critical or high-aspiration-risk patients.
Never **force the tube** if resistance is met.
Listen carefully for signs of **respiratory distress** during insertion.
Always **verify tube placement** before administering anything through the tube.
Change the tube as per **policy or doctor's prescription** (often weekly).
Ensure a **communication system** (e.g., pen and paper, bell) is available for the patient if they cannot speak.

sections.title: Feeding the patient using a naso-gastric tube (PEX 2.1.10 - Continued)

blocks.text: Naso-gastric feeding can be given in two ways
**Intermittent feeding:** Given at intervals as ordered by the doctor (e.g., four hourly).
**Continuous drip:** Given as a continuous infusion over a specified period (e.g., 24-hour period).

**Feed bowl of warm water:** If feed needs warming
**Cup with warm water:** For rinsing the tube
**50 ml syringe barrel or funnel:** With tubing and connection appropriate for the tube
**Vomit bowl (kidney dish):** Ready at hand
**Mackintosh cape and towel:** Or dressing mackintosh
**Stethoscope:** For checking placement
**Spigot or clamp:** To occlude the tube after feeding
**Patient's chart:** For feed verification and charting
**Waste receptacle:** For safe disposal
**Bedside**
**Hand washing equipment:** Sink, soap, water, and towel
**Screens:** For privacy

blocks.title: Naso-Gastric Tube Feeding Workflow
blocks.caption: Five-stage sequence for safe gravity-administered NG tube feeding.

steps.label: Position & Protect
steps.detail: Sit patient upright (45°–90°), apply mackintosh cape/towel, wash hands, and wear clean gloves.

steps.label: Verify & Flush
steps.detail: Test aspirate pH (1–4), auscultate 10–20 ml air, check distress, and flush 10–20 ml water.

steps.label: Warm & Prime
steps.detail: Warm feed to 37°C–38°C, pinch tube, attach barrel/funnel, and prime with 10–20 ml warm water.

steps.label: Gravity Feed & Rinse
steps.detail: Hold 12–18 inches high without pushing, refill before empty, then rinse 10–20 ml and spigot.

steps.label: Post-Feed Care
steps.detail: Keep upright 30°–45° for 30–60 minutes, clear equipment, wash hands, and document.

blocks.title: Step-by-Step Procedure and Rationales (NG Tube Feeding)
rows: **Step 1**
Observe the **general rules**.
Promotes adherence to **standards** and **patient safety**.
**Step 2**
Assist the patient to be in a **sitting-up position** (up to **90°** for conscious patients) or a **lateral position** if unconscious raised to an angle of about **45°**, ensuring comfort.
Promotes patient ability to **swallow** (if conscious) and reduces the risk of **aspiration** during feeding.
**Step 3**
Protect the patient's neck and chest with a **mackintosh cape and towel**.
Protects **bed linen** and the **patient's clothing** from spillage.
**Step 4**
**Wash hands** and put on **clean gloves**.
Minimizes the risk of **infection**.
**Step 5**
**a. Aspirate stomach contents:** Check **pH with litmus paper** (should be acidic, **pH 1–4**).
**b. Inject air:** Inject **10–20 ml of air** while listening over the stomach with a **stethoscope**.
**c. Observe for distress:** Watch for **coughing** or **cyanosis** during air injection.
**d. Flush the tube:** Flush with **10–20 ml of water** to check patency and clear any obstruction.
Confirms that the tube is still **in situ in the stomach** and is **not blocked**.
**Step 6**
Prepare the **feed**, ensuring it is at the **correct temperature** (**room temperature** or slightly warmed in a warm water bath to **37°C–38°C**) and check the **feed amount** as ordered.
Ensures **patient comfort** and prevents **discomfort or cramping**.
**Step 7**
**Pinch the tube**, remove the **spigot**, and connect the **50 ml syringe barrel or funnel** to the end of the NG tube.
Prevents **air entry** into the stomach.
**Step 8**
Pour **10–20 ml of warm water** into the syringe barrel/funnel to **prime the tube** and allow it to flow by **gravity**.
Ensures **patency** and clears any **residual material**.
**Step 9**
Pour the **prescribed feed slowly** into the syringe barrel/funnel, adjusting its height (**12–18 inches** above the patient) to control flow by **gravity**; **do not push the feed**.
Allows **gravity** to facilitate flow and prevents **overloading the stomach**, reducing the risk of **vomiting and aspiration**.
**Step 10**
As the feed level gets low, **add more feed before the syringe barrel/funnel completely empties**.
Prevents **air** from entering the stomach, which can cause **discomfort and distension**.
**Step 11**
After the feed has run through, **rinse the tube with warm water** (**10–20 ml** or as ordered) to clear any remaining feed.
Prevents **clogging** of the feeding tube.
**Step 12**
**Pinch the tube**, remove the syringe barrel/funnel, and **clamp** the end of the tube with the **spigot**.
Prevents **leakage** and **air entry**.
**Step 13**
Keep the patient in the **upright or semi-upright position** (at least **30°–45°**) for at least **30–60 minutes** after feeding.
Promotes **digestion** and reduces the risk of **regurgitation and aspiration**.
**Step 15**
**Clear away the equipment** and **wash hands**.
Maintains **cleanliness** and **infection control**.
**Step 16**
**Document the feeding** in full:

**Include:** Date, time, **type and amount of feed given**, **amount of rinse water**, **patient's tolerance**, **any complications** (e.g., nausea, vomiting, distension), and **confirmation of tube placement method used**.
Monitors **input and output** and ensures **continuity of care**.

blocks.text: Warning: **Never Push Tube Feeds:** Never force feed through the NG tube with a plunger; control flow strictly by **gravity** (**12–18 inches** above the patient) and never let the barrel empty completely, to prevent **air distension**, **vomiting**, and **aspiration**.
Always **verify tube placement before each feeding** or medication administration.
Never **push feeds** into the tube using the plunger of the syringe; allow **gravity to control the flow rate**.
Keep the patient in a **semi-Fowler's or Fowler's position** during and after feeding.
Monitor the patient for signs of **intolerance** such as nausea, vomiting, abdominal distension, diarrhea, or coughing.

**How to revise it:** connect each point to assessment, nursing diagnosis or care problem, intervention, rationale and evaluation.

perform-gastronomy-feeding.title: Perform Gastronomy Feeding
perform-gastronomy-feeding.excerpt: Gastronomy Feeding is feeding of a patient by means of an opening directly into the stomach through the abdominal wall.
headings: Methods of feeding via a gastrostomy
Procedure for administration of Gastrostomy feeding.

blocks.text: Gastronomy Feeding is feeding of a patient by means of an opening directly into the stomach through the abdominal wall.

They are commonly surgically inserted endoscopically through the abdominal wall, and held in place by an internal balloon or bumper and external fixator. Gastrostomy feeding is a successful method of enteral feeding providing daily nutritional requirements in specialist liquid form directly into a patient’s stomach via a flexible tube.
Inability to Swallow Safely
**Dysphagia:** Difficulty swallowing due to neurological disorders, muscular diseases, or structural abnormalities.
**Aspiration risk:** High risk of food or liquids entering the airway, leading to pneumonia.
**Esophageal obstruction:** Blockage of the esophagus due to tumors or strictures.
**Carcinoma of the esophagus:** Cancer of the esophagus.
**Strictures of the esophagus:** Narrowing of the esophagus, often due to inflammation or scar tissue.
**Birth defects of the mouth:** Congenital abnormalities affecting the mouth and swallowing ability.
**Esophageal atresia:** Congenital absence or closure of part of the esophagus.
**Problems with sucking or swallowing:** Difficulties in patients with debilitated diseases like stroke and dementia.
Prolonged Malnutrition
**Chronic illness:** Conditions such as cancer, Crohn’s disease, or cystic fibrosis leading to long-term nutritional deficiencies.
**Anorexia nervosa:** Eating disorder characterized by extreme food restriction.
**Severe weight loss:** Inability to maintain adequate weight and nutritional intake.
Impaired Digestion & Absorption
**Short bowel syndrome:** Significant reduction in the length of the small intestine, hindering nutrient absorption.
**Malabsorption disorders:** Conditions affecting the ability to absorb nutrients, such as celiac disease.
Delayed Gastric Emptying
**Gastroparesis:** Delayed stomach emptying due to neurological or muscular dysfunction.
**Delayed gastric emptying due to medication:** Certain medications can slow down gastric emptying.
Coma or Altered Consciousness
**Severe brain injury:** Loss of consciousness or inability to swallow safely.
**Chronic vegetative state:** Persistent unconsciousness without awareness or purposeful movement.
Chronic Vomiting or Reflux
Severe gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD): Persistent vomiting and acid reflux leading to malnutrition.
**Intractable vomiting:** Persistent vomiting despite medical treatment.
Premature Infants
**Premature birth:** Infants born before 37 weeks of gestation may have underdeveloped digestive systems and require supplemental feeding.
**Failure to thrive:** Infants who fail to gain weight or grow adequately.
**Operations of the upper gut:** Procedures involving the alimentary canal, mouth, nose, and esophagus may necessitate gastrostomy feeding to allow for healing and recovery.

sections.title: Methods of feeding via a gastrostomy

blocks.text: **Bolus feeding:** A volume of liquid feed given usually via a gravity set over a short duration, e.g. 15–20 minutes. The feed is usually delivered via a gravity set, relying on the force of gravity to push the feed into the stomach.

**Continuous feed:** This is a feed given via an electronic feeding pump, which allows clinicians and home caregivers to deliver set amounts of enteral formula in a consistent manner, over a desired duration of time. The pump regulates the rate of feed delivery, ensuring a consistent and continuous flow into the stomach.
Feeding tubes are classified based on their length and retention mechanism:
A. Long Tubes

**Percutaneous Endoscopic Gastrostomy (PEG):** A long, flexible tube inserted through the abdominal wall and into the stomach. Placed endoscopically, meaning a thin, flexible tube with a camera is used to visualize the stomach and guide the tube placement. Offers a more minimally invasive approach compared to surgical placement.
**Long Balloon-Retention Tube:** A longer tube with a balloon at the end that is inflated within the stomach, securing the tube in place. Commonly used for individuals requiring longer-term feeding.
**Malecot Tubes:** A type of long tube that may be used for short-term feeding and is often used for drainage.
B. Skin-Level Tubes
**Firm Silicone Mushroom Retention:** These tubes have a mushroom-shaped end that rests against the stomach lining, preventing accidental tube removal. Examples include Bard feeding tubes.
**Balloon Retention:** These tubes have a balloon near the end that is inflated inside the stomach, securing the tube in place. Examples include AMT MINI and MICKEY feeding tubes.

Maintain patient safety and clinical standard
Wash hands and check temperature of the feed.
To prevent the spread of infection.
Aspirate and measure the stomach content before giving the feed.
To ensure feeds are absorbed.
Pinch proximal end of the gastronomy tube and connect funnel after removing the spigot.
To avoid air entry into the stomach.
Pour 10mls of water into the funnel, let it run through the tube slowly and followed by a prescribed amount of feed. Rinse the tube with 10m Is of warm boiled water.
To ensure patent tube throughout the procedure.
Pinch and disconnect the funnel when feeding is over and replace the spigot.
To prevent air entry into the stomach and backflow.
When the wound has not yet healed carry out gastrostomy toilet i.e. clean skin around the tube with normal saline and apply a protective cream e.g. Zinc Oxide and cover with dry dressing.
To promote healing and prevent infection.
Record the type, food amount given, and time.
Monitor input and output.
Provide oral hygiene, clean equipment and leave the patient comfortable.
To prevent infection to the patient.
Clear the trolley and wash hands.
To prevent cross infection.

blocks.text: 1. Tube-Related Complications
**Tube Obstruction:** Blockage of the tube due to thickened feed, medications, or debris.
**Primary Malposition:** Incorrect initial placement of the tube.
**Perforation of the Intestinal Tract:** A hole in the intestinal wall caused by the tube.
**Secondary Displacement of the Feeding Tube:** The tube coming out of the stomach or moving out of position.
**Knotting of the Tube:** The tube becoming tangled within itself.
**Accidental Tube Removal:** The tube being pulled out of the stomach.
**Breakage and Leakage of the Tube:** The tube becoming damaged and leaking.
**Leakage and Bleeding from Insertion Site:** Fluid or blood leaking from the opening where the tube enters the skin.
2. Site-Related Complications
Erosion, Ulceration and Necrosis of Skin and Mucosa: Damage to the skin and lining around the gastrostomy site.
3. Gastrointestinal Complications
**Intestinal Obstruction (Ileus):** A blockage in the intestines.
**Hemorrhage:** Bleeding from the stomach or intestines.
4. Systemic Complications
**Inadvertent IV Infusion of Enteral Diet:** Accidental injection of the feeding formula into a vein.
**Infection at the Tube Insertion Site:** An infection at the point where the tube enters the body.
**Aspiration Pneumonia:** Inhaling food or liquid into the lungs.
**Nasopharyngeal and Ear Infection:** Infection of the nose, throat, and ear.
**Peritonitis:** Inflammation of the lining of the abdominal cavity.
**Infective Diarrhea:** Diarrhea caused by infection.
5. Metabolic Complications
**Electrolyte Disturbances:** Imbalances in the levels of electrolytes, such as sodium, potassium, and chloride.
**Hyper- and Hypoglycemia:** High or low blood sugar levels.
**Vitamin and Trace Element Deficiency:** Lack of essential vitamins and minerals.

Use **Gastrostomy Feeding** as a practical nursing topic, not only a memorized definition. Turn the topic into practical nursing knowledge: meaning, assessment, care priorities, teaching and evaluation.
**What to understand first:** define gastrostomy feeding, identify the normal or expected pattern, then explain what changes when the patient is unwell.
**Why it matters in care:** the nurse must recognize risk early, explain findings clearly, document accurately and know when to escalate.
**How to revise it:** connect each point to assessment, nursing diagnosis or care problem, intervention, rationale and evaluation.

Findings that are normal, abnormal or urgent.
Resources, referral needs and documentation requirements.

Provide clear care, education and escalation when needed.
Evaluate response and record what changed.
The rationale for these priorities is patient safety: nursing actions should prevent deterioration, reduce discomfort, support recovery and create clear evidence for the next caregiver.
**Expected outcome:** The topic is understood in a way that supports safe nursing judgement and revision.
Explain gastrostomy feeding in simple language the patient or caregiver can repeat back.
Teach warning signs, medicine or follow-up instructions, hygiene or lifestyle points where relevant.

carry-out-gastric-lavage.title: Carry Out Gastric Lavage
carry-out-gastric-lavage.excerpt: Gastric lavage is the process of cleaning out stomach contents.

blocks.text: Gastric lavage is a gastrointestinal decontamination technique that aims to empty the stomach of toxic substances by the sequential administration and aspiration of small volumes of fluid via a nasogastric tube or stomach tube.

Gastric lavage is the process of washing out of the stomach via a nasogastric tube or stomach tube. Lavage is ordered to wash out the stomach (after ingestion of poison or an overdose of medication, for example) or to control gastrointestinal bleeding. If the patient does not have a nasogastric tube in place already, the physician will order the insertion of the appropriate tube.
General and Diagnostic Indications

**Ingestion of toxic substances:** Indicated when a patient has swallowed anything unwanted or poisonous, to remove toxic substances from the stomach before absorption into the **systemic circulation**.
**Pre-endoscopic procedure:** Performed to clear stomach contents before an **upper endoscopic procedure**, improving visualization during the examination.
**Collection of stomach acids for testing:** Used to collect **stomach acids** for diagnostic testing.

**Relief of gastric pressure:** Used to relieve pressure in the stomach when there is a blockage in the stomach or nearby areas such as the intestine, helping alleviate symptoms and prevent complications.

**Collection of sputum in children:** Useful for collecting sputum samples from children who cannot expectorate; it is a preferred procedure for children suspected of having **pulmonary tuberculosis**.
**Cooling technique in hyperthermic patients:** Used to lower body temperature in **hyperthermic patients** by irrigating the stomach with cool fluids.
**Diagnostic tool for gastric hemorrhage:** Used to diagnose inflammatory conditions such as **gastric hemorrhage** by examining the lavage fluid for the presence and severity of bleeding.

**Poisoning cases:** Commonly performed in **poisoning**—especially when life-threatening or when the patient's history is unavailable—to remove toxic substances from the stomach and reduce poison absorption.
Specific Substance Ingestions
**Potentially life-threatening substances:** Such as **chloroquine** and **cyclic antidepressants** (e.g., **amitriptyline**, **imipramine**).
**Substances not adsorbed by charcoal:** Ingestion of large amounts of substances not absorbed by **activated charcoal**, such as **iron** and **lithium**.

**Bezoar-forming substances:** Ingestion of substances with a propensity to form **bezoars** (a mass trapped in the **gastrointestinal tract [GIT]**), such as **iron** and **salicylates** (e.g., **aspirin** / **acetylsalicylic acid**).

Warning: **Airway and Perforation Risk:** Do not perform **gastric lavage** in patients who are **comatose**, **convulsing**, at risk of **gastrointestinal perforation/hemorrhage**, or who have ingested **corrosive substances** or **hydrocarbons/detergents**.

blocks.title: Contraindications to Gastric Lavage and Clinical Reasons
rows: **Comatose and convulsing patients**
Gastric lavage must not be performed on patients who are **comatose** or experiencing **seizures**.
**Ingestion of a corrosive substance**
Contraindicated when a **strong acid** or **strong alkali** has been ingested, as it can cause further damage to the **esophagus** and **stomach**.
**Pills too large for lavage tube**
If ingested pills or tablets are too large to pass through the **lavage tube**, gastric lavage should not be performed.
**Risk of hemorrhage or gastrointestinal perforation**
Individuals with pre-existing conditions that increase the risk of **bleeding** or **gastrointestinal perforation** must not undergo gastric lavage.
**Ingestion of hydrocarbons and detergent**
Contraindicated following ingestion of **hydrocarbons** (such as **ethanol**) and **detergent**.
**Non-toxic ingestion**
If the ingested poison is **not toxic at any dose**, gastric lavage is unnecessary.
**Adsorbed by charcoal within capacity**
If **activated charcoal** can effectively adsorb the poison and the ingested quantity does not exceed its **adsorption capacity**, gastric lavage may not be required.
**Delayed presentation**
If the patient presents **many hours after the poisoning incident**, gastric lavage may no longer be beneficial.
**Highly efficient antidote available**
If a **highly efficient antidote** is available for the ingested poison, gastric lavage may not be necessary.

blocks.text: Increase gastric delivery of tablets into the small bowel: Gastric lavage can potentially push tablets or pills further into the small bowel, increasing their absorption.

**Aspiration of gastric contents:** There is a risk of aspiration, where the gastric contents can enter the lungs, leading to respiratory complications. This occurs in approximately 3% of patients undergoing gastric lavage.
**Esophageal rupture:** Although rare, there is a risk of esophageal rupture during the lavage procedure.

**Cardiac complications:** In certain poisonings, such as those involving propranolol or calcium channel blockers, gastric lavage can precipitate extreme bradycardia, cardiac arrest, and asystole due to the effects on cardiac conduction.
**Nasal trauma:** Insertion of the lavage tube can cause nasal trauma.
**Tracheal intubation:** In cases where the airway is unprotected, tracheal intubation may be required before performing gastric lavage.
**Electrolyte imbalance and hypothermia:** The administration of large volumes of fluid during gastric lavage can potentially lead to electrolyte imbalances and hypothermia.
Clinical Pearl: **Clean Procedure:** **Gastric lavage** is a **clean procedure**; always verify gastric tube placement with **litmus paper** before instilling any lavage fluid.

blocks.title: Gastric Lavage Procedural Sequence
blocks.caption: Core nursing workflow from preparation through tube removal and documentation.

steps.label: Prepare & Position
steps.detail: Explain procedure, screen bed, prepare trolley, and sit patient up (or prone if unconscious) with mackintosh cape.

steps.label: Pass Stomach Tube
steps.detail: Lubricate tube and pass over tongue into pharynx and esophagus while encouraging swallowing.

steps.label: Confirm Placement
steps.detail: Aspirate stomach contents with syringe and test with blue litmus paper (turns red in acid).

steps.label: Instill & Siphon
steps.detail: Run ~300 mL fluid via funnel, invert into bucket to siphon, and repeat until return is clear.

steps.label: Withdraw & Document
steps.detail: Clip and withdraw tube evenly and quickly, clear equipment, wash hands, and document findings.

blocks.text: Warning: **Preventing Aspiration:** Keep the **stomach tube** disconnected from the **funnel and tubing** until after the tube has been passed and confirmed in the stomach, and keep a **suction machine** ready at the bedside if the patient is **unconscious**.
Step-by-Step Procedure and Rationales

blocks.title: Gastric Lavage Steps, Actions, and Rationales
rows: Follow general rules, collect needed equipment, and prepare the trolley.
Explain the procedure to the patient.
Screen the bed and close adjacent windows.
Bring the trolley to the bedside.
To enable cooperativeness.
To ensure privacy.
To prevent unnecessary movement.
Place a **bucket** on the floor at the bedside.
To collect wastes.
Request the patient to sit up if conscious.
If unconscious, position the patient **prone**.
Place a **mackintosh cape** and **towel** around the patient's neck and bedclothes.
To protect the bed and patient.
Connect the **funnel** to the **tubing** using a **connector**, keeping the **stomach tube** separate until it has been passed.
To prevent **aspiration** of fluid by the patient.
**Lubricate** the stomach tube and pass it over the tongue into the **pharynx** and **esophagus**.
To ease passage of the tube.
Keep asking and encouraging the patient to **swallow**.
To gain the patient's cooperation.
Connect the **syringe** to the tube and withdraw some stomach contents.
To ensure that the tube is in the **stomach**.
Test the aspirated stomach contents with **litmus paper** to confirm gastric placement.
Acidic stomach contents will turn **blue litmus paper red**.
Clip the **stomach tube** with an **artery forceps** and place it in the receiver.
To prevent **backflow** of stomach contents.
Apply a **clip** to the **funnel and tubing**, then attach it to the **stomach tube**.
To prevent the flow of fluids before starting the procedure.
Open the clip and allow approximately **300 mL** of fluid to run into the lower funnel until the level begins to rise.
Invert the funnel into the bucket to **siphon** out the stomach contents.
Repeat until the returning fluid is clear, noting the nature of the stomach contents.
To empty the stomach of unwanted or harmful contents.
Clip the **stomach tube** and withdraw it evenly and quickly.
Disconnect the tube from the funnel and tubing and place it in the receiver.
To prevent **trauma** to the patient.
Clear away all requirements and wash your hands.
Document: **type and amount** of lavage solution used; **appearance, odor, color, and amount** of gastric return; **patient's tolerance** to procedure; and **disposition of specimens**.

For accurate clinical documentation.

catheterization.title: Catheterization
catheterization.excerpt: Catheterization is the introduction of a fine plastic or rubber tube (catheter) through the urethra into the urinary bladder in order to remove urine or to

blocks.text: Define the term **catheterization**.
Name the **types of catheters** according to: Nature of procedure done (e.g., intermittent, indwelling)
Types of catheter (e.g., non-retaining, self-retaining, metallic, non-metallic, rubber, plastic)
State the **indications** for catheterization.
Identify the **requirements** for passing a urethral catheter.
Prepare the **requirements** for passing a urethral catheter.
Perform the **procedure** of passing a urethral catheter.
**Catheterization** is the introduction of a fine plastic or rubber tube (catheter) through the urethra into the urinary bladder in order to remove urine or to keep the urethra open.
Classification by Retention and Material
**Retention Type:** **Non-retaining** or **self-retaining** (e.g., **Foley catheter** with inflatable balloon).
**Material Composition:** **Metallic** and **non-metallic** (e.g., plastic, rubber, silicone).
**Rubber catheters.**
**Plastic catheters.**

blocks.title: Catheter Sizing (French Scale)
rows: **Children**
**Adult Females**
**Adult Males**
**General Range**

blocks.text: Clinical Pearl: **Select the smallest effective size on the French (Fr) scale** to minimize urethral trauma.
**Sterile Urine Specimen:** To obtain a **sterile specimen of urine** for examination or investigations (e.g., when a clean catch midstream sample is not possible).
**Urinary Retention:** To relieve **urinary retention** when other nursing measures have failed (e.g., after surgery, due to obstruction, or **neurogenic bladder**).
**Perioperative Bladder Emptying:** To ensure that the bladder is **empty before (pre-operatively), during, and after pelvic or abdominal surgeries** to prevent injuries to the bladder.

**Post-Void Residual Measurement:** To measure the amount of **residual urine** after voiding (**post-void residual**). It is done when partial obstruction of the bladder outlet is suspected (e.g., in **BPH**, **VVF** patients, patients on **bladder training**).
**Bladder Irrigation or Medication:** Emptying the bladder before giving a **bladder irrigation** or **installation of medication**.
**Urethral Splinting:** **Splinting the urethra** following urethral surgery or trauma.

**Urinary Incontinence:** In cases of **incontinence of urine** to prevent **bed sores** which may occur in diseases of the nervous system, trauma, and other conditions requiring strict **intake and output monitoring**.
**Critical Care Monitoring:** Monitoring accurate **hourly urine output** in critically ill patients.

blocks.title: Female Urinary Catheterization Workflow
blocks.caption: Core sequence from positioning and asepsis through insertion, balloon inflation, and closed-system drainage.

steps.label: Prepare & Position
steps.detail: Place patient in dorsal recumbent position with mackintosh/towel; prepare sterile pack and lubricate tip 2–4 cm.

steps.label: Glove & Cleanse
steps.detail: Don sterile gloves, drape, separate labia with non-dominant hand, and swab meatus anterior to posterior.

steps.label: Insert Catheter
steps.detail: With sterile dominant hand, advance lubricated tip 4–6 cm until urine flows, then advance 2–3 cm further.

steps.label: Inflate & Anchor
steps.detail: Inflate balloon slowly with 5–10 ml sterile water/saline and gently pull back until resistance is felt.

steps.label: Drain & Document
steps.detail: Connect closed drainage bag below bladder level, tape to inner thigh with slack, and document.

blocks.title: Female Catheterization Steps and Rationales
rows: Observe the **general rules**.
Promotes adherence to **standards**.
Assist the patient to adopt the **dorsal recumbent position** (lying on back with knees flexed and spread apart).
**Dorsal position** makes it easy for the nurse to carry out the procedure by exposing the **meatus**.
Place the dressing **mackintosh and towel** under the patient's buttocks.
To protect the bed linen from **urine spillage**.
**Wash hands** and put on **clean non-sterile gloves**.
Open the outer wrapper of the **sterile catheterization pack** and place on the trolley.
Open **sterile gloves** and place on the trolley.
Prevents **infection** and prepares the **sterile field**.
Pour **antiseptic solution** into a gallipot.
Open **sterile catheter** and place on the sterile area.
Draw up **sterile water/saline** into the syringe for balloon inflation.
**Lubricate the catheter tip** (about **2–4 cm**).
Maintains **sterility** and prepares the catheter for insertion.
Remove non-sterile gloves, **wash hands**, and put on **sterile gloves**.
Maintains **sterile technique**.
**Drape the patient's genitalia**, exposing the **urethral orifice**.
Place a **sterile receiver** on the drape between the patient's thighs to collect urine.
To create a **sterile field** and prepare for **urine collection**.
**Separate the labia** with the thumb and index finger of the **non-dominant hand** to visualize the **urethral meatus**; maintain separation throughout the procedure (this hand is now contaminated).
To visualize the meatus clearly and prevent contamination from the labia.
**Clean the urethral meatus** thoroughly with **cotton wool swabs** soaked in **antiseptic solution**, using the forceps.
Wipe from **anterior to posterior** (front to back), using a fresh swab for each stroke.
Clean from the meatus outwards and discard used swabs.
To prevent the introduction of **microorganisms** into the bladder.
Using the **dominant hand** (which is sterile), gently **insert the lubricated catheter tip** into the urethral meatus and advance slowly **4–6 cm** until urine begins to flow into the receiver.
Lubrication minimizes **trauma** to the urethra.
Gentle insertion prevents **injury**.
Length ensures entry into the **bladder**.
Once urine flows, **advance the catheter a further 2–3 cm** to ensure the balloon is fully within the bladder, holding the catheter in place with the **non-dominant hand**.
To ensure the **balloon is not inflated in the urethra**, which would cause pain and damage.
**Inflate the balloon slowly** with the pre-drawn **sterile water/saline** using the syringe (amount specified on catheter, usually **5–10 ml** for adult Foley).
To **secure the catheter** in the bladder and prevent it from slipping out.
Gently **pull back on the catheter slightly** until resistance is met, indicating the balloon is seated at the **bladder neck**.
Confirms **correct placement** and anchors the catheter.
**Connect the catheter to the drainage bag and tubing system**, ensuring a **closed system**.
Ensure the drainage bag is positioned **below the level of the bladder**.
To allow continuous **drainage of urine** and maintain a **closed sterile system** to prevent **infection**.
**Secure the catheter** to the patient's inner thigh with **adhesive tape**, allowing for some slack to prevent tension on the meatus.
Prevents accidental **dislodgement** and irritation of the urethra.
Dispose of used equipment and materials appropriately and **wash hands**.
Maintains **cleanliness** and **infection control**.
Leave the patient **comfortable** and check that urine is draining freely into the bag.
Provide **post-procedure care and instructions** to the patient (e.g., signs of infection, hydration).
To ensure patient **comfort** and well-being and prevent **complications**.

**Document** the procedure, including the date, time, type and size of catheter inserted, amount of fluid used to inflate the balloon, characteristics and amount of urine obtained (if initial drainage), patient's response, and name/signature of nurse.
For **continuity of care**, monitoring, and **legal record**.

blocks.text: Warning: **Never inflate the balloon until urine flows and the catheter has been advanced a further 2–3 cm** into the bladder; inflating in the urethra causes severe pain and tissue damage.

blocks.title: Male Urinary Catheterization Workflow
blocks.caption: Aseptic male catheterization sequence emphasizing perpendicular positioning, generous lubrication, and paraphimosis prevention.

steps.label: Prepare & Drape
steps.detail: Complete general prep (Steps 1–7), place supine with legs extended, and drape genitalia.

steps.label: Cleanse & Lubricate
steps.detail: Hold penis perpendicular (retract foreskin if present), swab circularly outward, lubricate 6–8 inches, and instill gel.

steps.label: Insert 15–20 cm
steps.detail: Insert gently during slow deep breaths until urine flows; never force against resistance.

steps.label: Inflate & Replace Foreskin
steps.detail: Advance 2–3 cm, inflate balloon with 5–10 ml, pull back gently, and replace foreskin.

steps.label: Secure & Document
steps.detail: Attach closed bag below bladder, tape to inner thigh or lower abdomen, and document.

blocks.title: Male Catheterization Steps and Rationales
rows: Follow the **general steps for catheterization preparation** as for a female patient (Steps 1–7 Female Procedure), including explaining the procedure, ensuring privacy, preparing equipment, and washing hands/donning sterile gloves.
The **principles of catheterization preparation** remain the same in both male and female patients.
Assist the patient to lie in the **supine position** with legs extended.
**Drape the patient's genitalia**, exposing the penis.
To provide **privacy** and easy access to the penis.
Using the **non-dominant hand** (now contaminated), **grasp the penis** just below the glans and retract the foreskin if uncircumcised.
Hold the penis **perpendicular** to the body.
To expose the **urethral meatus** and **straighten the urethra** for easier catheter passage.
**Cleanse the glans penis** with **cotton wool swabs** soaked in **antiseptic solution**, using the forceps.
Wipe in a **circular motion** from the meatus outwards, using a fresh swab for each stroke, and discard used swabs.
Maintain hold of the penis with the non-dominant hand.
To prevent the introduction of **microorganisms** into the bladder.
**Lubricate the tip of the catheter** (about **6–8 inches**).
**Inject some lubricant directly into the urethra** using the syringe (or use a pre-lubricated catheter).
Lubrication minimizes **trauma** and **friction** and helps the catheter pass through the longer male urethra.
Using the **dominant hand** (which is sterile), gently **insert the lubricated catheter tip** into the urethral meatus.
Ask the patient to take slow, deep breaths or bear down gently as if to void, and advance the catheter slowly.
Deep breathing helps **relax the external sphincter**.
Gentle insertion follows the natural curves of the urethra.
**Advance the catheter about 15–20 cm** until urine flows into the receiver.
The male urethra is longer than the female; ensures the catheter reaches the **bladder**.
If resistance is met, **do not force**.
Ask the patient to relax and breathe deeply; gently rotate the catheter or apply slight traction to the penis.
If resistance persists, **withdraw the catheter and consult the mentor or doctor**.
Forcing can cause **trauma**, **stricture**, or **false passages** in the urethra.
Relaxing can help the sphincters open.
Once urine flows, **advance the catheter a further 2–3 cm** to ensure the balloon is fully within the bladder.
To ensure the **balloon is not inflated in the urethra**.
**Inflate the balloon slowly** with the pre-drawn **sterile water/saline** using the syringe (amount specified on catheter, usually **5–10 ml** for adult Foley).
To **secure the catheter** in the bladder.
Gently **pull back on the catheter slightly** until resistance is met.
Confirms **correct placement**.
**Replace the foreskin** if it was retracted.
To prevent **paraphimosis** (foreskin trapped behind the glans).
**Connect the catheter to the drainage bag and tubing system**, ensuring a **closed system**.
Ensure the drainage bag is **below the level of the bladder**.
To allow continuous **drainage** and maintain a **closed sterile system**.
**Secure the catheter** to the patient's inner thigh or lower abdomen with **adhesive tape**, allowing for some slack.
Securing to the abdomen directs the catheter upwards, reducing pressure on the **penoscrotal angle** of the urethra.
Prevents accidental **dislodgement** and tension on the meatus.
Complete the procedure as per Steps 17–19 of the female catheterization procedure (dispose of equipment, wash hands, patient comfort, documentation).
Maintains **cleanliness**, ensures patient comfort, and provides a record.

blocks.text: Warning: **Never force a catheter past resistance** (risk of urethral **trauma**, **stricture**, or **false passages**), and **always replace the foreskin** after catheterization to prevent **paraphimosis**.
Catheterization is a **sterile procedure**; therefore, **strict aseptic precautions** must always be followed throughout the procedure. Any break in sterile technique should be corrected immediately.
The procedure should be performed with **extreme care** to prevent **trauma** to the delicate urethral and bladder organs.
Always **verify catheter placement** before inflating the balloon.
Never **force the catheter** against resistance.
Use **adequate lubrication**, especially for male patients.
Choose the **correct size catheter** to minimize discomfort and trauma.
Ensure the drainage system is always **below the level of the bladder** to facilitate gravity drainage and prevent backflow.
Provide **ongoing catheter care** (cleaning meatus, checking drainage, ensuring patency) to prevent **infection**.
Monitor the patient for signs of **complications** such as pain, bleeding, inability to pass urine, or signs of infection (fever, cloudy urine, foul odor).
Use **Catheterization** as a practical nursing topic, not only a memorized definition. Prioritize airway, breathing, circulation, pain, asepsis, wound healing and early complication detection.
**What to understand first:** define catheterization, identify the normal or expected pattern, then explain what changes when the patient is unwell.
**Why it matters in care:** the nurse must recognize risk early, explain findings clearly, document accurately and know when to escalate.
**How to revise it:** connect each point to assessment, nursing diagnosis or care problem, intervention, rationale and evaluation.
Vital signs, pain, bleeding, perfusion, level of consciousness and injury pattern.
Wound appearance, drainage, odour, swelling, temperature and surrounding skin.
Fluid balance, mobility, nutrition, surgical site risk and ordered investigations.
Stabilize urgent problems first, then prepare for investigations or theatre care.
Maintain aseptic technique, pain control, wound care and documentation.
Prevent shock, infection, pressure injury, deep vein thrombosis and delayed healing.
The rationale for these priorities is patient safety: nursing actions should prevent deterioration, reduce discomfort, support recovery and create clear evidence for the next caregiver.
**Expected outcome:** The patient remains stable, wound healing progresses, pain is controlled and complications are recognized early.
Explain catheterization in simple language the patient or caregiver can repeat back.
Teach warning signs, medicine or follow-up instructions, hygiene or lifestyle points where relevant.
For exams, prepare a short answer using: definition, causes or risk factors, signs, assessment, management, complications and prevention.
For ward practice, document baseline findings, actions taken, patient response and the plan for review.
